item.title: Some results of the Somali paremiological experiment in Berlin and Arhus
item.description:
Paper read at the 4th International Conference of Cushitic and Omotic Languages, Leiden, 10–12 April 2003.

Paremia is a Greek word which means saying, parable; paremiology refers to the philological branch of science dealing with proverbs, proverbial phrases and so on. The youngest branch of the science concerning proverbs, empirical paremiology, which operates statistical methods of analysis, is directed at the establishing of paremiological minima of different cultures. The paremiological minimum is a minimal set of proverbs, sayings and other paremias, the learning of which is necessary for the understanding of any language, whether native or foreign. The fact is that paremias not only decorate speech, but also serve as a convenient means of expressing typical real or thinkable situations, the signs and model of which they are.

item.title: Kinship Terms in Somali and Oromo: A Comparative Study
item.description:
Originally published in Исследования по языкам Африки, Выпуск 2 (2008)

Abstract

This study presents the first comprehensive comparison of kinship terminology systems in Somali and Oromo, two major Cushitic languages. Through systematic field research and analysis of 38 Somali kinship terms and corresponding Oromo equivalents from Borana and Arsi dialects, we establish both shared features and distinctive innovations that illuminate the historical relationships and cultural adaptations within the Cushitic language family.

item.title: On Somali paremias based on numbers
item.description:
Paper read at the 11th Interdisciplinary Colloquium on Proverbs, Tavira, 2017; published in ACTAS ICP17 Proceedings, ed. Rui J. B. Soares and Outi Lauhakangas. Tavira: AIP-IAP, 2018, pp. 70–78. Published here in full with the author’s permission.

I. The Somalis divide their paremias into two types: maahmaah a proverb and oraah a saying. My investigation of the Somali paremiological stock has enabled me to identify at least twelve types of clichés: six one-phrase clichés (proverbs proper, folk aphorisms, non-divided sentences, proverbial phrases proper, by-words and non-divided phrases) and six supra-phrase clichés (three types of wellerisms i.e. clichés containing a remark and the cue of a character and three types of scenes, i.e. clichés containing a dialog of characters).

item.title: Paremias without sentence particles
item.description:
Paper read at the 7th International Semito-Hamitic Congress, Berlin, 2004.

In his review of my first book Andrzejewski attracted the attention of linguists to

“archaic grammatical forms which, paradoxically enough, form part of everyday language and are commonly used in conversations and in the mass media. A good example of this are those verbal and verbal-adjectival forms which exclude the occurrence of focus indicators (baa, ayaa, waxaa and waa) in declarative sentences such as for example Ayax teg eelna reeb — Locusts go away but leave damage behind and Tuug wax ka tuhun badan — A thief is more suspicious than anyone else. In Kapchits’ collection 7 per cent of all the items contain such grammatical forms, while normally focus indicators are obligatory in all declarative sentences.”1

item.title: Introduction to European Proverbs
item.description:
Introduction to European Proverbs by Rui João Baptista Soares (Portugal) and Elena Carter (Russia). Tavira, 2018, pp. 21–24. Published here in full with the author’s permission.

According to Lord John Russell’s not quite scientific but surely brilliant definition, “a proverb is the wit of one and the wisdom of many.” The book “European Proverbs” by Rui João Baptista Soares (Portugal) and Elena Carter (Russia) familiarizes its readers with the proverbial wisdom of the people who speak Portuguese, English, and Russian using their most common sayings for the purpose of learning the Portuguese and Russian languages. In turn, English language proverbs may serve as a connecting link to illustrate the broad similarities of paremias1 used by many European nations.

item.title: The proverbs shown on this site
item.description:
One of these appears on the front page each time it is loaded. The whole set is listed here.

Two hundred and forty-nine of them are the Somali paremiological minimum: the proverbs that the paremiological experiment found to be known to more than half of the speakers questioned. They are given below in the order the experiment established, from the one proverb every single respondent knew down to those known to just over half. That percentage is the finding, and it is what makes this list something other than an anthology.

item.title: Scholars in the Country of Poets
item.description:
Notes on the 8th International Congress of Somali Studies (Hargeisa, July 3–13, 2001)

I

The Somalis affirm that the ancestors of the great Russian poet Alexander Pushkin lived in the Horn of Africa. They came from the Arab tribe, and that is why his great-grandfather, brought to Russia when a child, was named Peter the Great’s arap.1

In Hargeisa I was reminded of it by clever and charming Abdulkadir Haji Ismail Jirdeh, who combines a passionate love of poetry with the prosaic work of the speaker of the local parliament. We met in the house of the Head of Hargeisa University, Sheikh Ali Ibrahim, who arranged a party in honour of the participants of the Congress. Standing on the flat roof and sipping orange juice (there is a dry law in Somaliland) we were talking about everything, and of course, about poetry, which in the country of poets goes without saying. By that time I had spoken enough Somali and was conversing in Russian with pleasure — my interlocutor remembered perfectly well the language he learnt in Odessa once upon a time. It turned out that he paid the highest tribute to the second genius of Russia, Michael Lermontov, and knew his poem “Demon” by heart:

item.title: Conferences & Congresses
item.description:
Four decades of Somali studies conducted largely from Moscow meant that the field itself was met at congresses — in Mogadishu, Hargeisa, Leiden, Berlin, San Diego. What follows is the documented record of those appearances, with the papers given at each.

Somali Studies congresses

4th Congress of Somali Studies — Mogadishu, 1989. The first visit to Somalia, at the invitation of the Somali Academy of Sciences. Twenty years later the same city was revisited in a series of travel essays written for Voice of Russia.

item.title: Research Projects
item.description:
Behind the books there are four long-running lines of work. Each took years, and each produced something the field did not have before.

The paremiological experiment

The question sounds simple and had never been answered for any language of the Horn of Africa: which proverbs do Somalis actually know?

Collections tell you what editors have gathered. They do not tell you what is current. The method for finding out was developed by G. L. Permyakov, who established a “paremiological minimum” for Russian of some 300 items — the set genuinely known to most speakers.

item.title: Kinship Terms in Somali and Oromo
item.description:
Overview

Dr. Kapchits’ research on kinship terminology represents one of the most comprehensive studies of social organization in Cushitic societies. This work documents the complete system of 38 Somali kinship terms and provides comparative analysis with Oromo terminology.

The Somali Kinship System

Core Family Terms

Immediate Family

  • abbe - father
  • hooyo - mother
  • wiil - son
  • gabadh - daughter
  • nin - husband
  • naag - wife

Extended Family - Parental Generation

  • adeer - paternal uncle
  • abti - maternal uncle
  • eedo - paternal aunt
  • habaryar - maternal aunt

Extended Family - Grandparent Generation

  • awoowe - grandfather (paternal)
  • ayeeyo - grandmother (paternal)
  • awoowe - grandfather (maternal)
  • ayeeyo - grandmother (maternal)

Sibling Relations

Same Generation

  • walaal - sibling (gender neutral)
  • walaasha - sister
  • walaalkii - brother
  • ina-adeer - paternal cousin (male)
  • ina-abti - maternal cousin (male)

Affinal Relations (In-laws)

Spouse’s Family

  • soddog - father-in-law
  • soddoh - mother-in-law
  • xigto - sister-in-law
  • xigto - brother-in-law

Descendant Terms

Children and Grandchildren

  • caruur - children (collective)
  • oo - grandson/granddaughter
  • oo-oo - great-grandchild

item.title: The Guardian on the Hargeisa Book Fair
item.description:
In July 2012 The Guardian reported on the fifth Hargeisa International Book Fair under the title “Somaliland’s Hargeisa book festival celebrates fifth year”.

The festival — founded by Jama Musse Jama and described in the report as the Horn of Africa’s answer to Hay-on-Wye — was held in a workers’ club in the centre of the city, with ribbons in the colours of the national flag, tents selling watermelon, and armed guards at the gate. The report set out what the organisers were trying to do: preserve the oral tradition, fill a cultural vacuum left by two decades of collapse, and give young people something other than khat and recruitment by al-Shabaab. It described the work of setting up reading clubs and libraries across six regions.

item.title: “Somalis Do Not Use Proverbs to Lie”: Dr. Georgi Kapchits in the Horn Newspaper
item.description:
On 14 July 2012, at the 5th Hargeisa Book Fair, Dr. Georgi Kapchits presented his new Somali-language book Soomaalidu Been ma Maahmaahdo (“Somalis do not use proverbs to lie”). The following day the Horn newspaper published an interview with him, together with a report by Yusuf M Hasan.

At the Book Fair

The Somali language, with over 100,000 proverbs, is among the richest languages in the world. This was said by Dr. Georgi Kapchits during the interview in Hargeisa, where he also disclosed that the lengthy studies he has undertaken reveal that the Somali language has no proverbs for lies.

item.title: Drought in Somali Folklore
item.description:
A column (“Kolumni”) by Dr. Georgi Kapchits, first published in “Afrikan Sarvi / Horn of Africa Journal”, No. 1/2012, issued by Suomen Somalia-verkosto ry (Finnish Somalia Network).

‘From where rain was expected mist has come’, said one of the Somali ancestors, first looking at the pale sky and then at the herd of camels which he had just brought from the half empty Well of the Last Hope. ‘A she-camel which has not drunk water for thirty days will endure three days more’, answered his brother, trying to soothe him. ‘But what shall I do with them’, asked he, pointing at his sheep and goats which were hiding themselves under the tree from the hot rays of the Sun at its zenith. ‘A drought is coming’, uttered the first one.

item.title: The Traveller to Legendary Lands
item.description: An interview conducted by Georgi Kapchits and published on WardheerNews on Sunday, 12 April 2009; WardheerNews re-posted it on 31 January 2015, and it was reprinted in the anthology KAYDSO: Qoraalladii Warsidaha BADSO 2014–2017 (pp. 265–273). item.title: The Country of Poets and Pirates
item.description:
In May 2009 the Voice of Russia observer Georgi Kapchits returned from Somalia where he served as an interpreter and consultant for a Russian television crew. He visited numerous parts of this formerly integrated country, met with political leaders and cabinet members, as well as fishermen, pirates, city residents and rural villagers.

In recent years, the fractured nation-state of Somalia, which occupies a vast territory on the Horn of Africa, has become notorious for the scandalous activities of local pirates who have captured dozens of trade vessels in the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean, then received millions of dollars in ransom money to relinquish the cargo ships and their crews. The amounts of money received by such marauders and their collaborators sometimes exceed the annual operating budgets of the current governments of Somaliland, Puntland and a shrunken “Somalia.”

item.title: Lamberti's Maps of Somali Dialects and the Current Socio-Linguistic Situation in South Somalia
item.description:
A study of Somali dialectology and its application to the language analysis of asylum seekers. The typescript bears no date; since it refers to an applicant who left Somalia in 2007, it cannot be earlier than that year — the dating given here is approximate.

I

In 1981 Marcello Lamberti undertook a scale research work in Somalia which resulted in a series of pioneering publications on Somali dialects. In “The linguistic situation in the Somali Democratic Republic” (1984), “Map of Somali dialects in the Somali Democratic Republic” (1986) and “Die Somali-Dialekte” (1986) he drew, as justly mentioned by Andrzej Zaborski, “a clear picture of dialect differentiation and dialect spread of the Somali language.”

item.title: Men and Women in the Somali Narrative Folklore
item.description:
The paper for the Buranbur conference in San Diego — 3 March 2007.

I am going to remind you of some Somali proverbs about women, their role in the traditional society and their relationships with men. Each proverb carries a message of the Somali ancestors to the present generation of the Somalis. Some of them are very funny and I hope you will enjoy them.

According to the following proverb, men are desperate about women. They say: Naago ama u samir, ama ka samir — Either suffer from women or suffer without them. But men understand that they badly need them: Naag waa belaayo loo baahan yahay — Woman is a disaster one cannot do without.

item.title: On Some Peculiarities of the Somali Language, Proverbs and Folktales
item.description:
The paper for the Buranbur conference in San Diego — 3 March 2007.

I

Somali is a very rich language from the point of view of phonetics, syntax and vocabulary. In its “Northern variant” (maxaad tidhi) it is a tonal accent language. The main classes of words in Somali are nouns and verbs.

Some words with attributive meanings belong to the class of verbs: dheer — to be long, cad — to be white, etc. The majority of words with adverbial meaning belong to the class of nouns: hoos-ta — bottom, si-da — mode, mean.

item.title: The WardheerNews Interview (2006): Selected Passages
item.description:
On 25 January 2006 the website WardheerNews.com published a long interview with Dr. Georgi Kapchits, conducted in Somali by Isamail A. Hassan (“Khaliil”). Dr. Kapchits was staying in Berlin at the time, working on his dictionary of Somali proverbs. The interview was picked up by other Somali websites and became one of the most widely read pieces WardheerNews published that year.

The full Somali original is reproduced here: Wareysigii ay mareegtada WardheerNews la yeelatay Dr. Georgi Kapchits.
